I’m thrilled to announce that PropertyKindCalculus (PKC) is officially open-source! :rocket:
(from my linkedin post: https://lnkd.in/p/gp8-WXbk)

Repo: https://lnkd.in/ggq5ixDG
Docs: https://lnkd.in/g3tymPZw

Developed at NASA JPL, PKC provides a rigorous metrological foundation for proving quantity and unit laws in Lean. We built this to bridge the gap between formal mathematics and real-world measurement, and I’m excited to invite the Lean PhysLib community to explore how we can collaborate.

If we want a robust formalization of physics in Lean, we need more than just a taxonomy of units—we need a true calculus. PKC is built natively on mathlib and offers a few key features that could significantly accelerate PhysLib:

:carpenter_square: Strict Categorical Foundations: Models "Dimension as a Forgetful Functor" and builds on Dybkær's ontology, where the comparability of properties is a fundamental primitive.

:earth_africa: ISO/IEC 80000 Complete: Ships with the entire standards catalogue formalized, from Mechanics and Thermodynamics to Electromagnetism and Atomic Physics.

🛠 Solves the Edge Cases: Rigorous handling of the Dimension-1 problem, complex-valued carriers, and scale-spanning units.

:bar_chart: Measurement Uncertainty: Native support for uncertainty quantification and numerical adequacy.

:high_voltage: "Write once, correctly & go fast, automatically": Via TorchLean, PKC enables the compilation of formal physical models to execute directly on CPU (Lean compilation) or GPU (TorchLean CUDA kernels). You verify the physical equations with metrological quantities exactly once, and the execution scales automatically.

I’d love to get feedback from the formal verification community—especially those involved in PhysLib. Could PKC serve as the metrological spine for our shared physics formalizations? Let's build the future of verified physics together!

Is there a file here which you would recommend looking at first, which shows what this system can actually do?

Strict Categorical Foundations: Models "Dimension as a Forgetful Functor" and builds on Dybkær's ontology, where the comparability of properties is a fundamental primitive.

This makes me happy on one side: I like categories. But worried on another side: Historically when we have used categories in the past in Physlib, it has led to maintenance problems. Do you explicitly use Lean's categories, or is it more that this is the underlying philosophy?

PKC imports no Mathlib.CategoryTheory. The categorical content is there as vocabulary plus coherence laws proved as ordinary lemmas. Since we recently refactored Physlib's Unit and Dimension, these are the ones that should be directly relevant:

  • DimensionedKind.toDimension — the forgetful map on objects, with the two coherence laws toDimension_times / toDimension_unitless: dim preserves the multiplicative (monoidal) structure and the unit.

  • InteractionAlgebra.dim_homomorphism — the capstone: whenever the kind algebra sanctions a × b = c, dim c = dim a * dim b. That is what licenses forgetting down to the dimension layer without losing soundness.

The load-bearing fact is the other direction: dim is not injective at dimension one, which is the whole reason the kind layer exists.

There is one place where we use a Mathlib categorical structure directly — a Quiver of quantity-kind relations in a metrological provenance graph (instance : Quiver (IncidenceVert g)). Vertices are the graph's nodes and occurrences; a node enters an occurrence at each operand position it fills — one arrow per position, so occurrence multiplicity is definitional — and an occurrence exits to its result. Quiver.Path is then the derivation chain at full incidence resolution, and on an acyclic graph the hom-sets of the path category are finite types (isAcyclic_incidenceQuiver, finite_incidencePath) — which is what makes an uncertainty budget a well-formed finite sum over paths.

The general lemmas underneath that (Quiver.IsAcyclic, length_lt_card, finite_path, Path.arrows_injective) are written in Mathlib's own namespace with an upstream target recorded in the header: ForMathlib/Combinatorics/Quiver/Acyclic.lean. Happy to PR it if it looks useful.

Two questions back:

  1. Would you expect the dim forgetful map to be worth stating as a CategoryTheory.Functor? Its laws here are two rfls, so the instance would buy vocabulary rather than proof, and I would rather learn from you whether that pays for itself than guess.

  2. ForPhysLib/README.md is our write-up of what PKC does and where it might pertain to Physlib — it has a "how to read it in ten minutes" section. The part I would most like your opinion on is one design question about the carrier. Is there a topic where that belongs, or would you rather it go to an issue?

@Nicolas Rouquette many thanks for this. I haven’t had chance to read this fully yet. But just as a reminder that LLm generated messages are banned on the Zulip - which this reads like. If you can write things in your own words that is much better!

To answer your questions:

  1. I would avoid using Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Functor if possible. I think it likely isn't needed.
  2. I think this could belong in this discussion.

Looking at this line. 

@[kindIngest]
def velocityAtQ (xₜ : Time → E1) (t : Time) : Quantity velocityK ℝ :=
  .attest "the trajectory's time derivative, component 0" (∂ₜ xₜ t 0)

could you summarize what .attest and what the types involved are? Is the idea behind .attest that it adds the ''physics context" if so - how does it effect the use of velocityAtQ?
